REVIEW: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds “Human Best Friend”

By Connor Schwigtenberg

-

August 6, 2026
Facebook
X
WhatsApp
Linkedin
ReddIt
Email
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 7:13
    Instaread

    This Thursday’s episode of Star Trek: Strange New Worlds sees our characters seek out their own journeys, both physical and spiritual. The crew have earned a spot of shore leave, which quickly goes off the rails. Focusing in on Ortegas (Melissa Navia) and Scotty (Martin Quinn), can they drag everyone back to reality before disaster ensues? Or will the crew be trapped partying forever with the Enterprise left in ruin?

    Written by Kathryn Lyn, who’s penned shamelessly silly episodes like “A Space Adventure Hour“ and “Charades“, we’re in for a wild ride. In the director’s chair is Yana Gorskaya, who’s a newcomer to Star Trek, but has extensive comedy experience. When Strange New Worlds swings to a new genre, they excel at getting the right people behind the camera to make it a reality.

    WARNING – Spoiler discussion below for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4 Episode 3 “Human Best Friend”

    Party Planet and Hangovers

    The episode opens with a childish rivalry between Ortegas and Scotty. A petty argument that doesn’t belong on the bridge of the Federation’s flagship. The series’ use of character drama to drive the plots brings it out of step with much of the franchise’s history, making Starfleet look less utopian and professional than it otherwise appears. Romantic subplots have been littered throughout previous seasons, to varying success, but this prank war feels like it crosses a line, even for Strange New Worlds.

    As tensions reach a boiling point for the ship’s alpha shift, Pike (Anson Mount) orders the crew take some much needed shore leave. The advertisement for the planet is littered with references to both The Original Series and The Animated Series. Fans can have fun pointing at the screen and recognising things. However, it’s all cheap key jingling to disguise the fact there’s nothing particularly original or compelling in this setup.

    After some psychedelic visuals and the crew giggling like maniacs, we’re thrust into the main episode. Ortegas and Scotty wake up together with no recollection of how they got there. They need to work together to solve the mystery, wasting an entire episode’s character development on a feud that was started for no discernible reason. The plot being an excuse for a tour of the show’s cast playing under the influence fails to give this any urgency, stakes, or a compelling reason to keep watching.

    Plant Friends and Mind Melds

    The rest of the main cast are shown in varying stages of intoxication. Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding) is stuck as a hippie, resorting to cheap stereotypes about journeys and connections. Pike gets a regrettable tattoo, and Number One (Rebecca Romijn) embarrasses herself at karaoke. The drugs effect everyone differently, much like the real thing. However, the effects are so different that it fails to create rules, seemingly as an excuse to swing between stereotypes about drunk, stoned, or tripping for a cheap gag.

    The only one who gets a real arc is Spock (Ethan Peck), who’s hallucinating but somehow grounded enough to be useful. We see a new aspect of Vulcan physiology, mind melding with a plant in a sequence so frustratingly silly. It’s so cringeworthy that if it didn’t progress the plot, I’d try to ignore it. They also thought him hallucinating plants was funny enough to do more than once, which it’s not. The only thing he doesn’t hallucinate is Kirk (Paul Wesley) who’s awkwardly forced into another episode.

    At least here, they pretend to develop the friendship between the pair. The end result is something that doesn’t want to commit to the popular Spirk ship, but also doesn’t create a compelling reason these characters are close. Of course the canon says they are, but we’re given no insight into why, which is the one thing a prequel is supposed to afford the audience. I did laugh at Kirk saying he’ll eventually go back to his own ship, albeit not for the reasons I think the show intended. Inserting Kirk is increasingly a hindrance to the show’s stories, rather than the intriguing guest star he should be.

    Civil Wars and Fireworks

    The final third of the episode is taken up by a bomb plot. For no reason other than artificial stakes, the danger never manages to feel real. With the crew back on the ship, there was a surprise that the episode still had so long to go. Without buildup, I felt nothing watching What follows is the predictable endpoint of forcing Ortegas and Scotty together – ending the needless rivalry. With the crew still under the influence, hungover and trying to work, they need to defuse the situation themselves.

    The sacrifices they’re willing to make are touching, even if Scotty’s plot armour does take away from the finale’s stakes. Swapping to Ortegas holding the bomb fixes all of these problems. Although at least the shared experience ends the rivalry these characters had for no real reason. Resolving conflict that had no reason to exist became the focal point of an entire episode. It’s a waste of time that could’ve been spent actually developing these characters, rather than resolving petty squabbles.

    The detonation, in full view of the alien delegation, resolves that plotline neatly. Even the saboteur who put the bomb there is resolved in a throwaway line at the end. It’s a lazily neat bow on a climax that was thrown together just to manufacture stakes. With the rest of the episode being a mystery box of nothing, the conclusion is just forced and deeply unsatisfying. Much like behind hungover in the real world, the episode went on too long and isn’t particularly enjoyable.

    Conclusion

    Breaking viewer trust in the crew’s professionalism and manufacturing cheap conflict goes against the entire philosophy of The Original Series. Other entries are freed of this problem, but as a prequel, Strange New Worlds‘ insistence on drama is jarring. A take on The Hangover is a fine idea, but it amounts to a series of sketches about different substances. Stripping that away, “Human Best Friend” leaves us with little more than character drama that was forced to begin with.

    I wish there was more praise I could level at this than the cast seeming to have a good time. Manufactured dangers and lazy plotting make the season’s shortest episode so far feel far longer. Drug gimmicks and predictable character arcs only carry an episode so far. The competency behind and in front of the camera makes it far from offensive. But with Trek‘s rich televisual history, it’s far from the franchise’s strongest hours. Hopefully next week’s film noir-based outing makes for enjoyable viewing.

    Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4 streams on Paramount+ in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, and Australia. It’s also available on SkyShowtime in select European markets and on TVNZ in New Zealand. Premiering on July 23 2026, it will air episodes weekly on Thursdays, concluding on September 24.
